listing.title: Turquoise Properties Ltd v Zoobair and Osman Properties Ltd

text:
Turquoise Properties Ltd v Zoobair and Osman Properties Ltd

2026 INT 287

THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF MAURITIUS
(Civil Division)
In the matter of:
CN 683/24
Turquoise Properties Ltd
Plaintiff
v.
Zoobair and Osman Properties Ltd
Defendant
RULING
1. The Plaintiff is suing the Defendant for having fraudulently and illegally claimed
VAT from the Plaintiff. In his proecipe, the Plaintiff avers that the Defendant has
received Rs 1.8 M as VAT in relation to a lease agreement entered into by the
Plaintiff and Kensons Hotel Ltd and as such, the Defendant was not entitled to
claim VAT on the said transaction.
2. In his plea, the Defendant raised a plea in limine litis which reads as follows:“1. The plaint discloses no cause of action against the Defendant.
2. In the alternative the plaint is time barred and all interested
parties have not been put into cause.
For the above reasons, the Defendant moves that the present
action be dismissed. With costs.”

1

 3. Learned Counsel for the Defendant informed court that he would not argue the
issue of time bar for the moment as evidence would have to be adduced first.
During the course of the arguments, Learned Counsel for the Defendant also
dropped the first limb of the plea in limine altogether. Hence, only the issue of
non-joinder of interested parties was argued.
4. I have duly considered the submissions offered by Counsel on both sides as
well as the authorities referred to.
3. It is trite law that only interested parties need to be joined as parties to a case,
that is, only parties whose presence is necessary for the court to determine the
questions in controversy and whose rights are likely to be affected by a
judgment of the court. Vide the cases of Cellplus Mobile Communications
Ltd v Gellé & Ors [2001 MR 193] and Ramgoolam (Dr) (GCSK, FRCP) v
Hurdoyal & Ors [2021 SCJ 394].
5. The definition of an “interested party” is given in the case of Mooradally v.
Gunessee & ors [2025 SCJ 62], where the Supreme Court cited with approval
the case of Ramgoolam (Dr) (GCSK, FRCP) v Hurdoyal & Ors [2022 SCJ
116]. The extract reads as follows:-

“The definition of an “interested party” has been examined ... as a
person “whose presence is necessary to ensure that all matters in
dispute in the cause or matter may be effectually and completely
determined and adjudicated upon; or whose interest may be affected
by the result of the present proceeding; or to ensure that the judgment
has “l’autorité de la chose jugée” in relation to them.”
6. It is further highlighted by the Supreme Court, in the case of Front Patriotique
Rodriguais v The Electoral Commissioner & Anor [2017 SCJ 40], that “It is
a fundamental rule of fair hearing that any decision, which would inevitably
impact upon the rights of ...parties, cannot be taken behind their back and
without giving them any opportunity to take a stand.”

2

 7. This court also stands guided by Rule 19 of the Supreme Court Rules 2000
which finds its application here, being given the silence of the District,
Industrial and Intermediate Courts Rules 1992 on the issue of joinder of
parties. The Rule 19 of the Supreme Court Rules provides as follows:“19. Addition and substitution of parties
(1) Any misjoinder or non-joinder of parties shall not defeat any cause
of action and the Court may deal with the matter in controversy so far
as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it.
(2) The Master or the Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, on
the application of any party and on such terms as may appear to the
Master or to the Court to be just, order the names of a party who(a) has been improperly joined be struck out;
(b) ought to have been joined, or whose presence before the Court
may be necessary in order to adjudicate upon and settle all questions
involved in the case be added.”
8. It is clear from the above provision that the non-joinder of a party is not fatal to
a suit. The court may still hear the matter and adjudicate on the rights and
interests of the parties before it. The court may also, on the application of any
party, order the joinder of any interested party. However, it is now well settled
that such joinder cannot be ordered by the Court proprio motu, in the absence
of an application by any party. See Mungur v. The Municipal Council of
Quatre Bornes [2023 SCJ 77].
9. In the present matter, the averments in the proecipe are to the effect that
Plaintiff signed a lease agreement with Kensons Hotel Ltd on the 17 th of May
2011 for a duration of 57 years and 11 months and for a consideration of Rs 12
M. Kensons Hotel Ltd was represented by one Mr Mohammad Zoobair Dawood
Timol. Prior to the signature of the lease, the Plaintiff made several payments
and for which it received receipts emanating from one Z & O Properties Ltd,
now believed to be the Defendant. Upon the signature of the lease, Kensons
3

 Hotel Ltd confirmed that the full amount of Rs 12 M has been paid by the
Plaintiff. On or about the 3rd of October 2014, Plaintiff received an unsigned
invoice bearing the letterhead of the Defendant, also represented by
Mohammad Zoobair Dawood Timol, requesting the Plaintiff to pay an amount
of Rs 1.8 M as VAT on the lease of Rs 12 M. Believing the VAT claim to be
genuine, Plaintiff effected the payment of Rs 1.8 M to the Defendant and a
receipt was accordingly sent to Plaintiff by the Defendant. The Plaintiff later
became aware that the Defendant is a different legal entity from Kensons Hotel
Ltd. By virtue of his proecipe, the Plaintiff avers that the Defendant was not
entitled to claim the amount of Rs 1.8 M as VAT on the lease of Rs 12 M, which
was signed with Kensons Hotel Ltd, and that the VAT claim was hence
fraudulent and illegal.
10. Since the issue of non-joinder of an interested party is being canvassed in
limine litis, all the above averments of the proecipe are deemed admitted for
the purpose of this argument. The issue which this court will have to determine
therefore is whether, ex facie the proecipe, Kensons Hotel Ltd is a party whose
presence is necessary for the court to effectively and completely adjudicate
upon the matters in controversy between the Plaintiff and the Defendant.
11. Based on a perusal of the plaint, I find that the present claim against the
Defendant derives from a contractual situation, here the lease agreement,
between the Plaintiff and Kensons Hotel Ltd. In order to determine the ultimate
issue, which is whether the Defendant fraudulently claimed VAT on the said
lease agreement, it is important for the court to be enlightened as to the
relationships and dealings between the Plaintiff, Kensons Hotel Ltd and the
Defendant, the more so that some payments were made to one Z & O
Properties Ltd. The court must have the benefit of the whole picture to make an
effective determination of all issues in controversy, namely, it must look at the
basis on which the VAT claim was made, at whether VAT was indeed payable
to Kensons Hotel Ltd, at the capacity in which Defendant purported to act when
it claimed the VAT and the circumstances surrounding same, and at whether
Kensons has been unlawfully deprived of its property when the VAT was
claimed by the Defendant.
4

 12. It is therefore clear that all the issues in controversy will not be fully addressed
in the absence of Kensons Hotel Ltd. The present claim cannot hence be looked
at in isolation without giving Kensons the opportunity to take a stand in the
matter. Moreover, the rights and interests of Kensons Hotel Ltd are likely to be
affected by a judgment in the present matter, since it will settle whether the
Defendant was legally entitled, or not, to claim VAT on the amount of the lease
agreed between the Plaintiff and Kensons Hotel Ltd. The presence of Kensons
Hotel Ltd will thus ensure that the judgment has “l’autorité de la chose jugée” in
relation to it and prevent a subsequent dispute from arising out of the same
subject matter. I therefore do not agree with the submissions of Learned
Counsel for the Plaintiff that Kensons Hotel Ltd can simply be called to testify
as a witness during trial.
13. In the light of the above, I find that the joinder of Kensons Hotel Ltd is necessary
to enable the court to determine all relevant issues in the presence of all parties
whose rights may be affected.
14. Since no application has been explicitly made for the joinder of Kensons Hotel
Ltd as a party, I call upon the Plaintiff to take a stand in the light of the present
ruling (Re case of Mungur (supra)).

14th October 2026

Y. NATHIRE BEEBEEJAUN
Magistrate
Intermediate Court

5
